tagline: River hamlets and cliffside curves on a highway completed in 1939
intro: NY 97 follows the Delaware River corridor between Hancock and Port Jervis, with wooded stretches, river hamlets and tight curves above the water. The Upper Delaware Scenic Byway joined the New York State Scenic Byways System on August 6, 2002. Its byway organization highlights rolling hills, long vistas and rock formations along the 70-mile drive.

The legislature laid out a river route in 1911, but much of the highway still had to be built. Construction advanced during the 1920s; two sections remained unfinished when the NY 97 number was assigned in 1930. The Route Ninety-Seven Council campaigned to give the entire road one number, opposing a proposed NY 17L designation; the state chose NY 97 in June 1939. The whole highway opened on August 30, 1939, with a ribbon-cutting in Port Jervis and a motorcade along its length.

Driving south from Hancock, the road winds through woods before reaching Long Eddy and Hankins. Railroad tracks accompany it into Callicoon and through parts of Cochecton before Narrowsburg. Farther south, Minisink Ford brings the crossing at Roebling's Delaware Aqueduct, followed by Barryville and Pond Eddy. The Hawk's Nest carries the road along cliffs overlooking the Delaware before the final approach to Port Jervis.

moments.title: Callicoon
moments.text: Callicoon was a transport center before it was a railroad depot: the Delaware carried lumber toward coastal cities to the south and east. In the 1840s, the Erie Railroad followed the riverbanks through the community, which took the name Callicoon Depot. A fire destroyed much of the business district in 1888, and rebuilding cost the town much of its earlier architecture. The last scheduled passenger train left in 1966. By the late 1960s, campgrounds and canoeing had helped tourism become the main industry. Downtown became the Callicoon Downtown Historic District, added to the National Register of Historic Places in 2016.

moments.title: Roebling's Delaware Aqueduct
moments.text: Canal boats once crossed above the Delaware here at Minisink Ford. The canal ferry had created a bottleneck and collisions with timber rafts heading downstream. Russell F. Lord and John A. Roebling designed the replacement aqueduct, which opened in 1849. After the canal closed in 1898, the aqueduct was drained and converted for vehicles. It is the oldest existing wire suspension bridge in the United States, but its canal appearance includes later reconstruction. The National Park Service rebuilt the superstructure in 1986 and reconstructed the towpaths, aqueduct walls and wooden icebreakers in 1995.

moments.title: Hawk's Nest
moments.text: The tight bends of the Hawk's Nest run along cliffs above the Delaware, a few miles north of Port Jervis. A cliffside road had linked this river corridor since at least 1851, before the modern highway’s construction. Early plans for the improved highway would have taken it along the shoreline instead. The Erie Railroad refused to sell the necessary right-of-way, so the state built along the cliffside. This section cost $2 million of the $4 million spent on NY 97. The winding road has overlooks into the Delaware River Valley.
